quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: In a vault carved into a mountain on a remote island, more than a million seed samples from almost every country are stored at minus eighteen degrees. The purpose of this seed bank is not to supply farmers but to serve as insurance: if a war, disease or disaster destroys a national collection, the original can be replaced from copies. In 2015, that scenario became real when a research centre in Syria asked for its seeds back after its own facility was damaged in the conflict. It was the first withdrawal, and the centre used the returned seeds to rebuild its collection of wheat and barley varieties suited to dry climates. Some experts note that the vault protects only seeds that can survive freezing and that many tropical crops must be kept alive as living plants. Even so, the vault remains a rare example of international cooperation that requires little day-to-day management. The site was chosen because the surrounding rock is stable and remains frozen even without power, and access is restricted to a few authorised staff. Each depositor keeps ownership of its own boxes.
quests.question: Why did the Syrian research centre request seeds?
options: Farmers demanded completely new varieties of wheat
It wanted to introduce tropical plants to its fields
Its own collection had been threatened by conflict
The vault was closing and needed the seeds moved
quests.correctAnswer: Its own collection had been threatened by conflict
quests.hint: Connect the purpose of the vault with the circumstances of the request.
quests.explanation: The vault exists as insurance for damaged national collections, and the centre's facility was damaged in conflict. Tropical crops are a limitation mentioned separately.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Dear passengers, we are sorry that your crossing on Friday was cancelled at short notice. The vessel developed an engine fault shortly before departure, and although engineers worked through the night, safety inspectors would not approve it for sailing. We arranged a replacement ferry for Saturday morning, but we recognise that this did not help those who had to travel earlier. Everyone affected will receive a full refund, and passengers who incurred expenses, such as an additional night in a hotel, can claim up to one hundred and fifty dollars on production of receipts. Claims should be submitted within thirty days through our website. The company will publish the inspection report on its website and contact all affected passengers by email within a week, so nobody has to wait for news. We will also offer a fifteen percent discount on your next booking. We appreciate that no amount of compensation replaces a lost day, and we are reviewing our maintenance schedule so that similar faults are found sooner.
quests.question: What does the ferry company promise to do to prevent similar cancellations?
options: Replace all its vessels
Employ more safety inspectors
Arrange more Saturday sailings
Review its maintenance schedule
quests.correctAnswer: Review its maintenance schedule
quests.hint: The promise about the future appears in the last sentence.
quests.explanation: The only preventive action mentioned is a review of the maintenance schedule so that faults are discovered earlier.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Open-plan schools, with large shared spaces instead of separate classrooms, were fashionable in the 1970s and fell from favour when teachers found that noise and distraction made lessons difficult. Recently, however, architects have rediscovered the idea in a modified form. New designs combine a large central area with small, quiet rooms that can be opened or closed, and their supporters argue that the difference lies in flexibility: pupils can work together on projects, then withdraw to concentrate. Studies of one such school found that pupils reported greater independence, though their test scores did not differ from those of similar schools. Teachers also said that the design suited some subjects, such as art and science projects, better than others. The lesson, according to the researchers, is that a building cannot substitute for good teaching, but can make certain kinds of teaching easier. Some teachers said they had to work harder at first to manage groups, though most agreed that the shared space made it easier to collaborate with colleagues. The building also uses far less heating because the rooms share warmth.
quests.question: What was the difference in test results at the new open-plan school?
options: Scores were much higher than at similar schools
Results were not measured at any stage of the study
Scores were much lower than at similar schools
There was no difference from similar schools
quests.correctAnswer: There was no difference from similar schools
quests.hint: Find the point where independence and scores are contrasted.
quests.explanation: Pupils felt more independent, but scores matched those of similar schools. The researchers conclude a building cannot replace teaching.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: The price of coffee on world markets has more than doubled in two years, and roasters are passing the increase to shoppers. Poor harvests in two of the largest producing countries, caused by drought and frost, are the main reason. Yet the growers' share of the retail price has barely moved. A cup that costs five dollars in a city cafe contains perhaps ten cents' worth of beans, and most of the rest covers rent, labour and profit. Many farmers also face rising costs, since fertiliser and transport have become more expensive, and older growers say that young people no longer want the work. Some companies have begun to sign long-term contracts that guarantee a minimum price, which gives farmers the confidence to invest in replacing old trees. Campaigners welcome this, but say that such contracts cover only a small part of the world's supply. In the meantime, some cafes have reduced the size of their cups rather than raise prices, hoping that customers will not notice the difference. Others have added a small surcharge for alternative milks.
quests.question: Why have growers not benefited from higher retail prices?
options: Their share of the final price has hardly changed
The harvest was unusually large this year
They have refused every long-term contract offered to them
Cafes buy beans directly from the farmers themselves
quests.correctAnswer: Their share of the final price has hardly changed
quests.hint: Look for the sentence beginning with "Yet".
quests.explanation: Retail prices rose, but growers' share remained small, while their costs also rose. Contracts help only a few.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A supermarket's loyalty scheme appears to be a gift to customers: points for every purchase and personalised discounts. But the arrangement is not one-sided. In exchange, the company gains detailed information about what people buy, when and where, which it uses to decide what to stock and how to price goods. A shopper who buys nappies, for example, may soon receive coupons for baby food. Critics point out that such tailored offers can encourage spending that customers had not planned. Supporters answer that shoppers are free to ignore the coupons, and that they benefit from lower prices. A survey found that most participants understood that data was being collected but few realised how detailed it was. Consumer groups now recommend that supermarkets explain clearly what they record and allow customers to opt out without losing their discounts. One supermarket has tried a different approach, giving customers a summary each month of the data it holds about them, together with a button to delete it. Early results show that few people press it.
quests.question: What did the survey reveal about participants?
options: They knew data was collected but not how detailed it was
They believed the scheme took data without giving anything back
They knew exactly what the supermarket recorded
They refused all the coupons they were sent
quests.correctAnswer: They knew data was collected but not how detailed it was
quests.hint: Find the survey sentence and note what participants did and did not realise.
quests.explanation: Most understood collection was taking place but underestimated its detail. The consumer groups' recommendation follows from that.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: Every morning, thousands of workers cross the border by train to jobs in the neighbouring country, where wages for the same work can be thirty percent higher. Employers there rely on them, particularly in hospitals and hotels, where they cannot find enough local staff. Yet the arrangement is fragile. Cross-border workers pay tax in one country and receive healthcare in the other, and a change in either country's rules can leave them out of pocket. During the pandemic, when the border closed, some lost income for weeks, and a few discovered that they were not entitled to benefits in either country. Since then, the two governments have agreed to coordinate rules, although details remain unsettled. Many workers say that they would like to stay in their own country but cannot afford to do so at local wages. Employers have started to offer language courses and help with transport costs, because losing staff to shorter commutes would leave gaps that are hard to fill. Trade unions say they need clearer, legally binding agreements.
quests.question: What problem did some workers discover during the pandemic?
options: They had to move permanently to the other country
They were forced to change jobs during the closure
Their wages were reduced by about a third
They were not entitled to benefits in either country
quests.correctAnswer: They were not entitled to benefits in either country
quests.hint: The problem appears in a sentence describing the border closure.
quests.explanation: Some cross-border workers fell between the two systems and could claim benefits in neither. The governments' response came afterwards.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Hospital waiting lists are often described as a single number, and politicians quote them as evidence of success or failure. But the figure hides a variety of situations. A patient waiting for a routine hip replacement is counted in the same list as someone waiting for an urgent diagnostic scan, though the two cases are very different. In addition, the total says nothing about how long people have been waiting; a list of ten thousand people who all wait a fortnight is very different from a list of ten thousand of whom a fifth have waited over a year. Health economists therefore prefer to report the proportion treated within a set time. This measure has drawbacks too, since managers may focus on patients close to the deadline while others wait longer. No single statistic captures the whole picture, they conclude, so several should be read together. One hospital that tried a single fixed target found that patients were being moved around the list in order to meet it, which made the numbers look better without improving care.
quests.question: Why do health economists prefer the proportion treated within a set time?
options: It removes the need for managers to plan capacity
It measures only urgent cases and ignores routine ones
It is easier for politicians to quote in speeches
A single total conceals different waiting times and situations
quests.correctAnswer: A single total conceals different waiting times and situations
quests.hint: The reason follows the criticism of the single number.
quests.explanation: The total does not reveal how long people wait or how urgent cases are. However, the alternative can also be manipulated.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Legal contracts are often written in a style that ordinary readers find impenetrable, full of long sentences and archaic phrases. Defenders of this language argue that it has been tested in courts for centuries, and that familiar wording reduces the risk of dispute. Others reply that a contract that one party cannot understand is a poor basis for trust. Some companies have experimented with plain-language versions, replacing "the party of the first part" with "we" and using short sentences and headings. In a trial, customers given the plain version were more likely to notice a fee and less likely to complain later. Lawyers remain cautious, since a simplified document may omit protections. The compromise emerging in practice is to keep the technical text but to add a plain summary at the start, making clear which parts matter most. A judge who reviewed the trial commented that clear language was not the same as weak language, and that the best contracts are those in which every clause can be explained to a client in a single sentence.
quests.question: What compromise is emerging in practice?
options: Allowing only lawyers to read the contracts
Keeping the technical text but adding a plain summary
Replacing all contracts with short handwritten letters
Removing legal language completely from every clause
quests.correctAnswer: Keeping the technical text but adding a plain summary
quests.hint: The compromise is announced with "emerging in practice".
quests.explanation: Companies keep the legal text and add a simple summary, satisfying both those who value tested wording and those who want clarity.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Peat, the dark soil dug from bogs, has been used in gardens for decades, valued for holding water and providing a light, rich mix for seedlings. Yet bogs are among the planet's most important stores of carbon, and digging them releases gas that took thousands of years to accumulate. Several governments have announced bans on peat compost, but gardeners' groups warn that substitutes, such as coir from coconut husks or composted bark, do not always work as well, particularly for delicate seeds. Manufacturers say that they are improving mixtures, but admit that alternatives cost more. Experienced gardeners suggest that the change is manageable if people adapt their habits, for instance by watering more often and making their own compost. A ban, they say, is likely to be easier for those who prepare than for those who resist. Garden centres report that sales of peat-free bags have doubled in three years, and some now sell only those. Nonetheless, professional growers still use peat for the most delicate crops, since they cannot risk failures.
quests.question: What do gardeners' groups warn about?
options: Alternatives may not work as well for delicate seeds
Composting is illegal in several of the regions
Peat is impossible to replace with anything else
Coir is more harmful to the environment than peat
quests.correctAnswer: Alternatives may not work as well for delicate seeds
quests.hint: Locate the sentence where the groups' concern is introduced by "warn".
quests.explanation: The groups fear substitutes may underperform, especially with delicate seeds. Manufacturers admit alternatives cost more.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Digitising an archive sounds simple: scan the pages and put them online. In practice, the work is slower and more demanding than most people expect. Old documents are fragile, and each page must be handled carefully; handwriting is often hard for software to read, so volunteers must transcribe it; and every item needs a description so that people can find it. A small local museum that began digitising its collection of photographs discovered that half of the images had no record of who was in them. It then invited residents to identify faces at an open day, and a lively discussion followed, filling gaps that no expert could have filled. The museum's curator believes that this collaboration may prove more valuable than the scans themselves, because it recorded knowledge held only in memory. Another problem was storage: digital files need to be copied regularly and moved to newer formats, otherwise they can become unreadable in a few decades. The museum has therefore agreed to keep paper originals as well.
quests.question: What does the curator consider more valuable than the scans?
options: The care taken with fragile paper during scanning
The description written for every item in the collection
The community knowledge collected through identification
The software that reads difficult handwriting
quests.correctAnswer: The community knowledge collected through identification
quests.hint: The curator's opinion is introduced by "believes that".
quests.explanation: Residents supplied information that existed nowhere in writing, which the curator sees as more valuable than the digital images.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Many people look forward to retirement as a time of rest, but studies suggest that a sudden loss of routine can affect wellbeing. Retirees who fill their time with structured activities, such as volunteering or part-time work, generally report greater happiness than those who do not. Charities, which often struggle to recruit volunteers, have begun to target this group, offering roles that use previous skills. A retired accountant, for example, may manage a charity's books, while a former teacher helps with reading programmes. The benefits are mutual: organisations gain expertise, and volunteers gain a sense of purpose and social contact. However, the researchers stress that volunteering must be freely chosen; retirees who feel pressured or who take roles they dislike do not show the same improvement. Employers, too, have begun to notice, with several offering phased retirement in which staff reduce their hours over a few years instead of stopping abruptly. Early reports suggest that this eases the transition for both sides.
quests.question: What condition do researchers place on the benefits of volunteering?
options: The charity must pay a wage
The role must be freely chosen and enjoyed
The activity must take place daily
The retiree must have been an accountant
quests.correctAnswer: The role must be freely chosen and enjoyed
quests.hint: The researchers' caution follows "However".
quests.explanation: People pushed into unwanted roles do not benefit in the same way. Skills matching is only an example.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Speed cameras are designed to make drivers slow down, but their effect depends on where and how they are used. Studies show that accidents fall sharply near a camera, yet some drivers brake hard just before the device and accelerate afterwards, which can create hazards a few hundred metres away. Average-speed cameras, which measure the time taken between two points, avoid this problem because drivers must keep to the limit along the whole stretch. On one motorway, deaths fell by almost a third after they were installed. Opponents claim that cameras are meant to raise money, though in many areas the income must be spent on road safety. A more persuasive complaint is that cameras do not address other causes of accidents, such as tiredness or phone use, which no camera can detect. Some countries publish the location of every camera in advance, on the grounds that the goal is safety rather than punishment, and drivers who know where the cameras are tend to slow down for the whole route.
quests.question: What advantage do average-speed cameras have?
options: They photograph only the fastest vehicles on the road
They detect tiredness or phone use in drivers
Drivers must keep to the limit along the whole stretch
They raise more money than other cameras
quests.correctAnswer: Drivers must keep to the limit along the whole stretch
quests.hint: Find the sentence that begins with the type of camera and follows a problem.
quests.explanation: Because the time between two points is measured, braking only near a device does not help. Detecting tiredness is beyond any camera.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Every year, millions of tonnes of electronic waste are exported from wealthy countries to poorer ones, where the recovery of metals such as copper and gold is done by hand. Workers, often children, burn cables to remove plastic and inhale toxic fumes. International rules prohibit the export of hazardous waste, but exporters frequently label items as second-hand goods, since reuse is legal. Inspectors report that a container marked as working televisions may contain broken screens. Campaigners want stricter tests to prove that equipment functions before it leaves, and some manufacturers have begun to take back old devices for proper recycling. Critics, however, note that voluntary schemes cover only a fraction of the total. The underlying problem, they argue, is that dumping is cheaper than treating waste safely, and until that changes, regulation will always be one step behind. Some governments have set up certified recycling plants at home, but exporting remains far cheaper, so shipments continue. Researchers have started to track containers using hidden location devices to prove where the waste ends up.
quests.question: Why do exporters label waste as second-hand goods?
options: Manufacturers require every item to be exported
Second-hand goods are worth more than new ones
Reuse is legal, so it avoids the ban on hazardous waste
Workers demand reuse of all their equipment
quests.correctAnswer: Reuse is legal, so it avoids the ban on hazardous waste
quests.hint: Look for the "since" clause after the description of labelling.
quests.explanation: Rules ban hazardous waste but allow reuse, so mislabelling exploits the difference. Inspectors find broken items in containers of supposedly working goods.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: The cost of school uniforms has become a source of concern for parents. Some schools require items with the school badge, sold only by one supplier at a price several times higher than plain equivalents. A recent survey found that an average family spends over three hundred dollars per child each year, and that one parent in five had borrowed to pay for it. New government guidelines say that schools should limit branded items to a few, such as a jumper or tie, and should ensure that second-hand uniforms are readily available. Some head teachers welcome the changes, arguing that uniforms promote equality, but only if all families can afford them. Others believe that abolishing uniform would be simpler, although they acknowledge that this brings its own pressure to wear fashionable clothes. A parent group in one region has organised a free exchange where families can swap outgrown items, and it now distributes more than four thousand garments a year, mainly at the start of the term.
quests.question: What do the government guidelines advise?
options: Increase the price of jumpers with the school badge
Limit branded items and provide second-hand options
Ban uniforms altogether and let pupils wear anything
Require every family to use a single supplier
quests.correctAnswer: Limit branded items and provide second-hand options
quests.hint: Find the sentence where the guidelines are quoted.
quests.explanation: Schools are asked to restrict badges to a few items and make used uniforms available. Some head teachers even prefer abolition, but that is not the guidance.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: As banks close branches in small towns, residents face a dilemma. Online banking works well for those with reliable internet and confidence, but older customers, and people who deal mostly in cash, often prefer face-to-face service. Some banks have responded by sharing a "banking hub" with other institutions, where staff from several banks work at counters in a single building. Trials suggest that hubs handle most basic transactions and are appreciated by small traders who need to deposit takings. Yet they are open only on certain days in many places, and complex issues, such as a mortgage, still require travel. One mayor described how the hub in her town had helped a bakery owner deposit cash without a two-hour journey. The banks involved say they will keep the hubs open for at least three years and then review use. Local councillors say that the hubs are better than nothing, but that a permanent branch is a sign of a town's economic health, and that its loss may discourage new businesses from opening there.
quests.question: What do local councillors think of banking hubs?
options: They are used only by older people in the town
They discourage new businesses from opening
They are superior to a permanent branch in every respect
They are better than nothing but no substitute for a branch
quests.correctAnswer: They are better than nothing but no substitute for a branch
quests.hint: The councillors' opinion comes in the last sentence.
quests.explanation: The hubs help, but councillors say a permanent branch signals economic health. They do not claim hubs are equal.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: The supermarket's own-brand products have improved so much that many shoppers cannot tell them from branded equivalents. In blind tastings, cheaper versions of biscuits, pasta sauce and orange juice are often preferred. This should be good news, but manufacturers of branded goods complain that supermarkets copy their packaging, which confuses customers and reduces the value of their investment in advertising. In some cases, the company that makes the branded item also makes the own-brand version in the same factory, at a lower price. Regulators have received complaints but concluded that imitation is legal, provided that customers are not misled about the origin. Consumer groups, meanwhile, suggest that a resemblance on the shelf may lead buyers to assume equal quality when, sometimes, ingredients differ. They recommend that shoppers read the labels rather than trust the picture. Some manufacturers have responded by launching cheaper ranges of their own, which compete with the stores' versions. Retailers say that competition of this kind benefits shoppers, even if the boundaries between brands seem increasingly blurred.
quests.question: Why might buyers be misled by similar packaging?
options: The products are always made in another country
The labels are hidden behind the packaging
Blind tastings are unreliable for judging quality
They may assume the products are of equal quality
quests.correctAnswer: They may assume the products are of equal quality
quests.hint: Find the consumer groups' concern.
quests.explanation: Similar packaging suggests similarity, but ingredients can differ. Reading labels is their advice.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Tidal power promises energy from a source as predictable as the moon, yet few schemes have been built. The difficulty is cost. Dams across estuaries, which capture water as it flows in and out, are extremely expensive and can alter the habitat of birds and fish. Underwater turbines, which resemble wind turbines, are less disruptive, but they must withstand corrosion and the force of powerful currents. One project off the northern coast has been operating for six years and supplies electricity to about three thousand homes, an achievement its developers describe as proof of concept. Larger arrays are planned, though the industry needs government support to reach the scale where prices fall. In the meantime, engineers are experimenting with floating platforms that can be towed into position and removed for maintenance, which could reduce installation costs, although the technology remains at an early stage. Whether tidal power becomes a major source will depend less on technology than on whether investors are willing to wait.
quests.question: What will determine whether tidal power becomes a major source?
options: Investors' willingness to wait for lower costs
Improvements in the design of wind turbines
The habitat of birds in estuaries
The movement of the moon around the earth
quests.correctAnswer: Investors' willingness to wait for lower costs
quests.hint: The final sentence contains a comparison of two factors.
quests.explanation: The outcome is said to depend less on technology than on investors. The predictability of the moon is not a constraint.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A neighbourhood association in a large city has turned an empty lot into a shared garden. The land was owned by a developer who had no immediate plans, and the council agreed to a temporary lease on condition that the garden could be removed on ninety days' notice. Volunteers installed raised beds, a compost system and a small greenhouse, and many of the vegetables are donated to a food bank. Now, however, the developer has applied for permission to build flats. Residents are torn: the city needs housing, but they fear losing the garden's community. They have proposed that the building include a rooftop garden and that a portion of the lot remain open. The developer has said it will consider the idea, though it has not promised anything. A local school uses the garden for science lessons, and a retired carpenter has built a small shed for tools. The association has collected more than a thousand signatures asking the council to protect the site.
quests.question: Why can the garden be removed?
options: The food bank closed and no longer needs vegetables
The council changed its mind about the lease
The lease allowed removal on short notice
The garden was built illegally on the empty lot
quests.correctAnswer: The lease allowed removal on short notice
quests.hint: The conditions of the lease are explained early in the passage.
quests.explanation: The lease was temporary and could be ended on ninety days' notice, so the developer's plan puts the garden at risk.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: For most of history, people slept in two blocks, with a period of wakefulness between them. Records from medieval Europe mention a "first sleep" and a "second sleep", separated by an hour or two when people prayed, talked or visited neighbours. Historians believe this pattern faded as artificial lighting spread and evenings became longer. Modern sleep researchers point out that many people who wake in the middle of the night worry that something is wrong, though they may simply be following an older rhythm. In some cultures, including those with a midday rest, dividing sleep remains normal, and people show no signs of poorer health. What matters, researchers say, is that the total amount of sleep is sufficient. This does not mean that everyone should divide their sleep; consistent sleep and wake times remain a reliable basis for good health. But the historical evidence suggests that waking at night need not be a disorder, and that anxiety about it may be more harmful than the waking itself.
quests.question: What does the writer suggest about waking in the night?
options: It should be treated with medication straight away
It may be natural, and worrying about it can make it worse
It happened only in medieval times and never today
It is always a sign of a serious sleep illness
quests.correctAnswer: It may be natural, and worrying about it can make it worse
quests.hint: The conclusion is in the last sentence, combining the historical evidence and a warning.
quests.explanation: Waking can follow an older pattern and is not necessarily a disorder. Anxiety may do more harm.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A city has spent millions of dollars on a new bridge for cyclists and pedestrians, intended to connect two districts separated by a river. The bridge is beautiful, but during its first month, few people crossed it. Surveys revealed that the approach on one side runs through a poorly lit underpass which many people, especially women, avoid after dark, and that the route on the other side ends at a busy road with no crossing. The city plans to add lighting and a signalled crossing, at a cost of a further three hundred thousand dollars. Planners say the lesson is that infrastructure should be evaluated as a system: the most elegant structure fails if the roads leading to it are neglected. Some residents are less forgiving and ask why these problems were not foreseen. Similar disappointments have occurred elsewhere: a footbridge in another city was ignored for years because it led to a car park, and became popular only after a cafe opened at one end.
quests.question: Why did few people use the bridge at first?
options: The bridge was not attractive enough to visit
The river was too wide for most walkers
The bridge was closed to cyclists after opening
The routes leading to it were unsafe or inconvenient
quests.correctAnswer: The routes leading to it were unsafe or inconvenient
quests.hint: The surveys explain the problem with the approaches.
quests.explanation: A dark underpass and an uncontrolled road crossing discouraged use. The bridge itself was open and admired.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: When a small software company allowed its employees to set their own salaries within a published range, managers expected chaos. Instead, staff were surprisingly moderate. Those who asked for the top of the range were mostly people who had been undervalued in earlier years, and several who could have asked for more chose less, saying they felt uncomfortable earning more than colleagues. The policy also had unexpected effects on recruitment: candidates were attracted by the openness, and some were more willing to accept jobs for which they had less experience because they felt trusted. At first, some employees worried that colleagues would feel resentful, so the company held short discussions in which people explained their reasoning to a small group. Almost nobody chose to change their figure afterwards. After two years, turnover had fallen, though the founders admit that the approach may not suit larger companies. They stress that transparency, not the salary decision itself, was the key: people accepted the results because they could see how the range was set.
quests.question: What do the founders consider the key to the policy's success?
options: The size of the company and its offices
Transparency about how the salary range was set
The choice of the top of the salary range
The low level of staff turnover
quests.correctAnswer: Transparency about how the salary range was set
quests.hint: The founders' conclusion follows "They stress that".
quests.explanation: Openness about the range made results acceptable. The lower turnover is an outcome rather than the key.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: The rise of cheap flights has made it possible for people to travel across Europe for the price of a train ticket, and many towns have benefited. However, residents in some popular destinations argue that the benefits are unevenly shared. Visitors arrive for a weekend, spend money in a few restaurants and stay in apartments booked through websites, often owned by people who do not live in the city. Rents have risen, since landlords find it more profitable to host visitors than to sign long leases, and neighbours complain that their buildings have become temporary hotels. One survey of residents in a coastal city found that seven in ten felt that their neighbourhood had changed for the worse in the last decade, while only a small minority said they had benefited directly. Some cities have limited the number of nights a home can be rented, though enforcement has proved difficult. Tourism officials reply that limits reduce income and that the answer is to attract visitors who stay longer and spend more, not to reduce numbers.
quests.question: Why have rents risen in popular destinations?
options: Landlords earn more from visitors than from long tenants
Fewer people want to live in the popular areas
Tourism officials have set the level of rents
Cities have banned short-term rentals in every district
quests.correctAnswer: Landlords earn more from visitors than from long tenants
quests.hint: The cause is in the sentence beginning "Rents have risen, since".
quests.explanation: Hosting visitors can yield more than long leases, which reduces housing for residents. Limits exist but are hard to enforce.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A short story competition run by a library received more than two thousand entries, and the judges noticed a pattern. Nearly a third of the stories began with a character waking up, and many ended with the revelation that everything had been a dream. Judges say that such conventions are familiar to writers because they are easy, and that stories which stand out usually avoid them. The winning entry, by a retired postman, described a single conversation on a train, with no dramatic events, yet the judges found it more moving than stories full of action. Its author said that he wrote what he had noticed in forty years of listening to people. The library plans to publish the winning stories in a book, with the proceeds supporting children's reading programmes. The judges also observed that stories written in the present tense outnumbered those in the past tense by two to one, though they were divided on whether this mattered. Entries came from thirty countries.
quests.question: What does the judges' comment about conventions suggest?
options: Waking up is a poor opening in every case
Familiar devices tend to make stories less distinctive
Dreams are banned from all stories in the competition
Action stories cannot win prizes
quests.correctAnswer: Familiar devices tend to make stories less distinctive
quests.hint: Read the sentence about why writers choose conventions and what happens to stories that avoid them.
quests.explanation: Easy, familiar devices are common, so stories that avoid them stand out. The judges do not ban any device outright.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: A new blood test can detect early signs of several cancers before symptoms appear. In a trial of more than ten thousand people, it correctly identified about half of the cancers found in the following year, and false alarms were rare. Doctors are cautious, however. Half is a useful figure for a screening tool only if the cancers detected are those that would otherwise be found late, and the trial has not yet shown that treatment following early detection leads to better survival. There is also a risk that the test may find slow-growing tumours that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment. The researchers plan to follow participants for a further five years. Until then, the test is offered only in research studies, and people are advised not to seek it privately. The company that developed it has said it is not seeking approval for general use until the longer study is complete. Meanwhile, patient groups have urged the public not to be misled by headlines.
quests.question: Why are doctors cautious about the test?
options: It is not yet proven that early detection improves survival
It produces many false alarms in healthy people
It is too expensive for researchers to continue testing
It has never found a cancer in any of the participants
quests.correctAnswer: It is not yet proven that early detection improves survival
quests.hint: The doctors' reason is explained in the sentence starting "Half is a useful figure".
quests.explanation: The trial has not shown better survival after early detection, and some tumours may be harmless. False alarms were described as rare.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A number of towns have begun to rename streets that were named after people whose reputations have changed. Supporters argue that street names are an honour, and that honouring someone linked to slavery or cruelty is inappropriate. Opponents say that history should not be erased and that renaming causes real costs, such as the need to change addresses on official documents. Some councils have chosen compromises: keeping the old name but adding a sign explaining the person's history, or renaming only when the community requests it. A survey in one city found that residents were more likely to support changes when a local vote was held and when the new name recognised a local person. In one town, a street formerly named after a colonial governor was renamed after a local nurse, and the council reports that few residents have complained. Businesses on the street received free new stationery. The debate, one historian says, is less about the past than about who has the authority to decide what a community celebrates.
quests.question: What is the historian's view of the debate?
options: It concerns only the events of the distant past
It is a debate about signs and not about names
It concerns who has the power to decide how a community remembers
It concerns the cost of changing addresses on documents
quests.correctAnswer: It concerns who has the power to decide how a community remembers
quests.hint: The final sentence gives an opinion in a "less about... than about" structure.
quests.explanation: The debate is said to be about authority over what a community celebrates, not merely about the past.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Marta had run the family's bookshop for thirty years, and when online retailers arrived, she was told repeatedly that she would not survive. Instead of competing on price, she changed the shop into a place where people wanted to spend time. She added a cafe, hosted readings and asked customers for recommendations, which she displayed on handwritten cards. Sales of books fell slightly, but the cafe more than made up for it, and, importantly, customers began to talk about the shop to others. Other independent shops in the town have followed her example, and a small trail of cafes and second-hand shops now attracts weekend visitors. Marta has begun to mentor two young owners who want to open their own stores. Yet the success brought a difficulty: the rent, based on the shop's value, was raised by a third. Marta says she would not have chosen a different path, but she wonders whether landlords realise that the neighbourhood's charm is created by the tenants they price out.
quests.question: What difficulty followed the shop's success?
options: Book sales collapsed
Customers stopped recommending the shop
The cafe closed
The landlord increased the rent
quests.correctAnswer: The landlord increased the rent
quests.hint: The difficulty is introduced by "Yet".
quests.explanation: The shop's rising value led to a rent increase of one third. Book sales fell only slightly and the cafe compensated.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: In some countries, people can choose to have their organs used after death, but many do not register, even when they support the idea. To increase donation, several countries have changed the default: unless people opt out, they are assumed to agree. The rates of registration rose, though evidence suggests that the effect on actual donations is smaller, since families are usually consulted and may refuse. Countries with the highest donation rates often combine the default with other measures, such as specialist nurses who speak to families and hospitals that are equipped to manage donors. Ethicists debate whether presumed consent respects autonomy, but most agree that the important question is whether the system builds trust. If people fear that doctors will not try to save them, they may opt out in large numbers. Public information campaigns also matter, because misunderstanding is common: many people believe that a donor card affects the quality of hospital care, which is untrue and harmful to trust. Some countries also allow people to record a specific refusal.
quests.question: Why is the effect of presumed consent on actual donations smaller than expected?
options: Ethicists forbid the system in most countries
Families are usually consulted and may refuse
Doctors do not treat donors as carefully as other patients
Nobody registers because the process is too difficult
quests.correctAnswer: Families are usually consulted and may refuse
quests.hint: The explanation follows "since" in the second half of the sentence about registration.
quests.explanation: Even when someone is registered, families are consulted and may say no. Other measures help the highest-performing countries.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: When people are asked how well they can concentrate, most say they are above average, which, of course, cannot be true for everyone. Researchers call this overconfidence, and it appears in many areas, from driving to cooking. It matters when it leads people to attempt tasks that require more focus than they can give, such as writing messages while walking in traffic. Studies of multitasking have found that people who believe they are good at it tend to perform worse than those who admit its difficulty, partly because they switch between tasks so often that each is done less well. In one experiment, students who were asked to switch between two tasks made almost twice as many errors as those who did them one after the other, yet most of them said the experience had felt efficient. The practical advice is modest: single-task where possible, turn off notifications during work that matters, and accept that a brief pause is not a sign of weakness. Nothing suggests that our brains have become worse; the environment has become more demanding.
quests.question: What did the studies of multitasking find?
options: Multitaskers concentrate best on driving and cooking
Nobody can switch between tasks at all
People who think they are good at it tend to perform worse
Everyone performs equally well at multitasking
quests.correctAnswer: People who think they are good at it tend to perform worse
quests.hint: Look for the surprising relationship between belief and performance.
quests.explanation: Those who rated themselves as good multitaskers did worse than those who accepted its difficulty.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A city council has proposed replacing its street lighting with LEDs, which use less electricity and last longer. The savings are estimated at four hundred thousand dollars a year, and the project would pay for itself within six years. Astronomers and ecologists have raised concerns, however, since LEDs give a bluer light that scatters more in the atmosphere and can disturb insects and birds. The council has responded by choosing warmer-coloured lights and installing dimming controls that reduce brightness after midnight, when few people are outdoors. Some residents worry that darker streets will feel less safe, though studies have found no consistent link between brightness and crime. The council will trial the new lights in three districts and publish the results of a survey of residents before making a final decision. If the trial goes well, the council intends to use part of the savings for a fund to plant trees along the main streets. Opposition members have asked for the trial period to be extended to a full year.
quests.question: How has the council responded to ecological concerns?
options: By selecting warmer lights and dimming after midnight
By asking astronomers to run the trial themselves
By adding more lights to the darkest streets
By abandoning the project after the objections
quests.correctAnswer: By selecting warmer lights and dimming after midnight
quests.hint: The council's response follows "has responded by".
quests.explanation: Warmer-coloured lights and dimming reduce the effects on insects and birds. The project is going ahead as a trial.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: An expedition to measure the depth of a remote lake in the mountains expected a simple task. The team lowered a weighted line from a small boat, but it kept snagging on something at the bottom. When they sent down a camera, they found a forest of trees standing upright, still with their branches. The cold, oxygen-poor water had preserved them, and dating showed they had grown around eight hundred years ago, before the lake formed. A rockslide, probably triggered by an earthquake, had blocked a valley, and the rising water drowned the trees. The discovery has given scientists a record of the ancient climate, since the rings of the trees reveal decades of growth. Diving teams are now planning to take samples, though they must work carefully to avoid disturbing wood that has survived for centuries. Scientists have compared the rings of the drowned trees with those from living forests nearby, which shows that a series of very cold summers occurred at about the same time. Some rings are so narrow that they are hardly visible.
quests.question: What caused the lake to form?
options: A change in the climate
A rockslide blocking a valley
Melting of the trees
The team's weighted line
quests.correctAnswer: A rockslide blocking a valley
quests.hint: The cause is in a sentence about an earthquake and a blocked valley.
quests.explanation: A rockslide blocked the valley and the water rose, drowning the forest. Tree rings later became evidence of climate.
